summary: Teach algebraic vocabulary (expression, equation, inequality, term, coefficient, factor) as language a learner USES while doing and justifying maths, not as definitions to memorise. The load-bearing distinction is expression vs equation, which turns on the equals sign: an expression names a value; an equation is a statement that can be true or false, so it can be tested by substitution; an inequality uses <, >, ≤, ≥ and is also a statement that can be tested; at this level it is typically true for a whole range of values (e.g. 2a + 3 < 11 for a < 4), though some inequalities are true for all values or for none. Teach '=' relationally (both sides name the same value / balance), explicitly challenging the operational 'work out the answer' reading, and name terms, coefficients and factors on genuine expressions including negative signs.
misconceptions: Calls any algebra string an 'equation' and expects to 'solve' it, even with no equals sign (writes an expression when asked for an equation).
Reads '=' operationally ('= means work out the answer'), so rejects 8 = 3 + 5 or treats an equation as an instruction rather than a statement.
Conjoins terms / treats a letter as an object, so miscounts terms or reads 3a + 2b as a single quantity (or '5ab').
Treats an inequality as if it were an equation with a single answer, ignoring the range of values it describes.

activities.title: Build an equation from an expression (card-sort workspace)
steps: Start with 2a + 3 sitting on its own and say aloud whether there is anything to 'test' or 'solve' — establish that it just names a value.
Drag an '=' and the number 11 alongside it to form 2a + 3 = 11, and say what has now changed.

Sort a set of six cards into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (e.g. 2a + 3, 2a + 3 = 11, 2a + 3 < 11), pointing each time to the =, <, >, ≤ or ≥ as the deciding feature, or saying that no such sign is present for an expression.
Substitute candidate values of a into 2a + 3 = 11 to test whether the statement is true or false; confirm it is true only at a = 4.

Also do an Always / Sometimes / Never true card sort, TESTING each statement by substitution rather than trying to 'solve' it, and recognising that one counterexample rules out 'always' (and one true case rules out 'never'), but checking a few values alone cannot prove 'always' or 'never' — give a reason for those.
activities.insight: The equals sign turns an inert value (expression) into a statement that can be true or false (equation) and therefore tested; an inequality is also a testable statement, and here (2a + 3 < 11) it is true across a whole range of values (a < 4) rather than at a single answer.

activities.title: Read '=' as balance and sameness
steps: Using a balance scale (physical or depicted), show that both sides of an equation name the same amount.
Judge and discuss statements written in unfamiliar orders, e.g. 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = ___ + 2, deciding whether each is legitimate and what goes in the blank.
Explain to a partner why 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are NOT different statements despite one looking 'backwards'.
activities.insight: The equals sign asserts that both sides have the same value; it is not an instruction to 'produce the answer on the right', so reversed and two-sided equalities are perfectly valid.

activities.title: Name terms, coefficients and factors — keeping the signs
steps: On 5x − 2y + 7, box each term WITH its sign and count the boxes (three terms).
State the coefficient of x (5) and of y (−2), being explicit that the minus sign belongs to the coefficient, and name 7 as the constant.
Contrast 3a + 2b (two terms, cannot be combined) with 3a + 2a (like terms that can) to resist conjoining and the '5ab' error.
On 2(a + 3), identify it as an expression whose factors are 2 and (a + 3), and state what would turn it into an equation.
activities.insight: Terms are the parts separated by + and − (each carrying its own sign); a coefficient is the number multiplying a letter, signs included; factors are what is multiplied together — and a letter stands for a number, not a labelled object, so unlike terms cannot be merged.

activities.title: Justify the word you chose ('convince me')
steps: After labelling a card, answer 'how do you know it's an equation and not an expression?' by pointing to the deciding symbol and saying what it does.
Respond to a sceptical questioner who challenges sloppy usage, e.g. 'you called that an equation — convince me', and defend or correct the label.
Explain, for an expression you chose, what you would add to make it an equation and what you could then do that you cannot do now.
activities.insight: Precise algebraic language is a tool for reasoning: being asked to justify a label is intended to push the learner past surface pattern-matching to state what the deciding symbol (=, <, >) actually means — that an equals sign makes a testable statement of sameness, not just that a particular symbol is present.

checkQuestion: Put three cards in front of the child: 2a + 3, then 2a + 3 = 11, then 2a + 3 < 11. Say: 'You and a partner are checking work. Your partner wrote 2a + 3 and called it an equation. Talk me through whether that's the right word, what you'd actually call each of these three, and what you could DO with each one.' Then listen — do not offer the words yourself.
checkAnswer: 2a + 3 is an expression — it has no equals sign, so there is nothing to test; it just represents a value. 2a + 3 = 11 is an equation — a statement that can be true or false, so you can solve it (a = 4). 2a + 3 < 11 is an inequality — true for a range of values (a < 4). To turn the expression into an equation you set it equal to something.
